name: audit-interceptor
intent: Declare an audit policy at an invocation seam that records the actor, action, target, correlation id and both attempt and terminal outcome around a delegated operation, then sends the structured event to a dedicated integrity-protected sink, so security accountability is consistent without inline logging in every service.
problem: Security-relevant operations (privileged actions, state changes and access to sensitive data) must be attributable, but inline logging misses denied and failed attempts, varies in schema, can leak raw arguments and disappears with a rolled-back transaction. Teams also need to cover components they cannot modify without pretending that a proxy sees calls that bypass it.
context: Business or service tiers whose sensitive operations pass through an interceptable seam: container-managed beans, proxied service objects, ORM entity lifecycles, message endpoints or an HTTP pipeline. Audit selection must be declarative and uniform, while the sink has its own integrity and retention requirements (Secure Logger); the design must make mediation gaps, redaction, transaction coupling, failure policy, clock source and correlation propagation explicit.
benefits: Security-relevant events are recorded uniformly at one interposition point instead of scattered inline log calls; coverage is auditable as a list of bindings rather than discovered by reading every method.

Targets stay free of the audit concern: audited operations keep their signatures, do not depend on the sink and are enrolled by binding or annotation rather than by editing them, so auditing can be retrofitted onto existing components.
A single event schema (actor, action, target, outcome, correlation id) makes records comparable and correlatable across services and layers.

Because the interceptor sees the invocation before delegation and the result after it, it can record both the attempt and the outcome — including denials and failures that inline logging usually omits.
The audit policy (what is recorded, redaction rules, destination, retention, failure handling) lives in one place and can be changed without recompiling the audited code.
Pairs with Secure Logger: interceptor plus tamper-evident sink yields records that can be used as evidence against the party being recorded.
Enables regulatory compliance by providing immutable, attributable records of who did what and when — foundational for SOX, HIPAA, GDPR, and PCI-DSS audit trails.
Decouples audit concerns from business logic, allowing security officers to adjust audit policy without touching production business code.
tradeoffs: Every audited invocation pays for an extra call, event construction and sink I/O; on fine-grained methods this overhead can dominate the business work, so join points must be chosen (state changes and privileged operations) rather than applied blanket-wide.

Complete mediation is an assumption, not a property of the mechanism: self-invocation, non-managed objects, direct concrete-type calls and calls made before wiring or after configuration drift are silently unaudited, and the interceptor cannot detect its own gaps.

The interceptor and its binding become security-critical components: whoever can edit the annotation/pointcut configuration, reorder the interceptor chain or redirect the sink can disable, forge or misroute the audit trail.
Naive interception captures arguments and return values wholesale; credentials, tokens and personal data end up in the record unless an explicit redaction or whitelist policy is part of the design.

The fail-open/fail-closed decision cannot be avoided: if the sink is unavailable the operation either fails (availability risk) or goes unrecorded (accountability risk), and leaving the default implicit means a silent choice.

Transaction and lifetime coupling: writing on the business transaction makes records vanish with a rollback, writing outside it makes records survive failed operations, and holding a sink reference per interceptor instance can leak resources if it is not released with the target.

Async audit pipelines (e.g., outbox pattern) improve throughput but risk losing events if the queue drops; hash-chain ordering becomes complex in multi-worker environments without a single sequencing point.
Per-event cryptographic hash chaining adds compute overhead; batched or incremental hashing with scheduled validation is preferred over synchronous per-event checks.

participants.responsibility: Observes the invocation, builds the audit event from the invocation context (actor, action, target, arguments, correlation id), writes it to the sink and delegates to the target; decides whether the delegation happens at all for fail-closed policies.
The audited operation or component; performs the business function and stays unaware of auditing.
The structured record of one security-relevant invocation: who acted, on what, when, with which outcome and correlation id.
Receives and durably stores the events with its own integrity and retention guarantees; realised by Secure Logger when the record must be trustworthy against the recorded party.
Invokes the interceptor around the target call, supplies the invocation context (method, parameters, proceed hand-off) and orders the interceptor chain.
Declares which operations are audited, with which event class and redaction rules, and how audit failures are handled.
Invokes the audited operation through the interception seam; its identity (or the subject it is acting as) is what the audit record attributes the action to.

use_cases: Business-tier auditing of money-moving or otherwise regulated operations (fund transfer, order placement, claim submission): who requested it, on which object, when, and whether it succeeded.
Privileged administration surfaces (role changes, key rotation, configuration changes) where every sensitive operation must leave a record naming the acting principal.
Authentication and authorization outcomes: successful and failed logins, access-denial decisions and lockouts routed into the same audit pipeline instead of ad-hoc log lines.
Access-to-sensitive-data events (who read which patient/customer record) recorded at the gateway or service boundary to satisfy data-protection obligations.
Retrofitting auditing onto legacy components whose code cannot be modified, by wrapping the service object or binding an interceptor to its interface.
Middleware-level auditing of message endpoints and database calls in a business tier, correlating the caller's subject with the operation performed.
Financial API request interception (Spring Boot global request interceptors) capturing who accessed which endpoint, with what payload, and what outcome — satisfying SOX financial reporting controls.

Entity-level change tracking via ORM subscribers (e.g., EF Core SaveChangesInterceptor, TypeORM subscribers): automatically diff old vs. new property values on create/update/delete and emit audit envelopes without manual logging calls.
API gateway-level audit logging: capture every external API call with timestamp, user identity, endpoint, method, and outcome, correlating across microservices via X-Request-ID / traceparent headers.
Compliance reporting automation: generate audit-ready reports for SOX (~7-year retention), HIPAA (~6-year retention), GDPR (data residency-aware), and PCI-DSS from structured interceptor events.

Zero-trust data access trails: record every read of sensitive fields (PHI, PII, financial data) so data-protection obligations (GDPR Article 5 data minimization, HIPAA access logging) are demonstrably met.
Hibernate Envers: @Audited entity lifecycle changes create per-entity _AUD revisions at transaction commit; a custom revision entity/listener can attach actor or request metadata.
Django admin: django.contrib.admin.models.LogEntry records action time, user, object, addition/change/deletion and change_message for ModelAdmin activity.
Rails Audited: the audited ActiveRecord extension creates audit rows for model create, update and destroy callbacks, including changed attributes and optional acting-user attribution.
avoid_when: You need generic before/after interception or parameter adaptation rather than accountability: use the Interceptor pattern; Audit Interceptor adds a security-event schema, actor attribution and outcome semantics.
You need to copy every message to a monitor without changing the primary flow: use Wire Tap; Audit Interceptor records a security event around an invocation instead of duplicating message traffic.
You need a durable, tamper-evident audit destination: use Secure Logger; Audit Interceptor is the event producer and does not make a mutable sink trustworthy by itself.

Subscribers must react to published state changes rather than wrap a call: use Observer or domain events; Audit Interceptor is bound to an invocation seam and can record denied or failed attempts that never publish a state-change event.
A single operation in a small program needs one log line: write it inline or call the logging framework directly; interception indirection buys nothing.

You need provable coverage of every call including internal ones: interception cannot see self-invocation or direct concrete-type calls, so use a chokepoint (one gateway or mediator) or infrastructure auditing (database audit tables, OS/journald auditing or API-gateway logs).
The audited operation sits in a hot inner loop: audit the external boundary or state transition, or use sampling and an asynchronous pipeline instead of synchronous per-call writes.
anti_patterns: Bind the audit interceptor to everything (all getters, all methods) and drown the sink: records stop being meaningful, storage and latency costs explode, and the real security-relevant events are lost in the noise.
Audit only the attempt (or only the success): a record that never states the outcome cannot answer what happened, which is the only question an audit trail exists to answer.
Write credentials, session tokens or full payloads into the audit record — the audit trail becomes the largest concentration of sensitive data in the system, and a data-protection liability.

Treat the interceptor as the security boundary: it is a detective control, not an authorization decision point, and it is trivially bypassed when calls do not route through the seam (self-invocation, direct concrete-type use, unwired components).
Let the interceptor swallow target exceptions so the audit trail looks clean, silently changing the business semantics of the audited operation.
Keep the audit write on the business transaction so a rollback erases the security record of the very event it should be recording.
Use a mutable log file as the audit sink: an administrator or attacker who gains filesystem access can alter or delete records, destroying the evidentiary value of the audit trail.
Propagate correlation ids only on the synchronous path and lose them across async boundaries (message queues, background jobs), breaking end-to-end traceability.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: auditing is one concern, business behaviour another; the interceptor carries the first, the target the second.
Single responsibility per role: interceptor records, target performs, sink persists, binding selects.
Open/closed principle: new auditable operations are enrolled by binding, not by modifying the operation.
Accountability and defence in depth: auditing complements preventive controls (authentication, authorization) by making their outcomes visible after the fact.
Least privilege and information hiding on the audit channel: the interceptor appends records, does not edit them, and writes only the fields the event schema allows.
Immutability and tamper-evidence: audit records, once written, must not be alterable by the recorded party; achieve this via write-once storage, hash chaining, or cryptographic signing.
Correlation and traceability: every audit event carries a correlation id propagated from the outermost entry point, enabling end-to-end reconstruction of distributed processing paths.

Failure declaration: the system's fail-open or fail-closed posture for audit unavailability must be explicitly designed and documented per operation criticality, not left as an implicit runtime default.
best_practices: Define the audit event schema first (actor/subject, action, target, outcome, timestamp, correlation id, reason) and make every interceptor write exactly that schema. Treat the schema as the enforcement point for what leaves the interceptor.
Record the attempt and the outcome, including denials and exceptions, and propagate the correlation id so records join across layers and services.
Bind selectively: audit state changes, privileged operations and access to sensitive data; leave read-only, high-frequency calls out unless they are security-relevant.
Write to a dedicated append-only, tamper-evident sink with separate credentials from the business data store, and treat the sink as a separate failure domain.
Redact or whitelist parameters before they reach the event — never log credentials, tokens or raw personal data, and treat the event schema as the enforcement point.
Decide and document the failure policy (fail-closed for high-value operations, fail-open with alerting elsewhere), and monitor for gaps such as unbindings, sink outages and interceptor exceptions.
Keep the audit write out of the business transaction (or use a separate one) so business rollbacks cannot remove security records.
Prune the interceptor chain deliberately: audit should wrap (not be wrapped by) authorization so denied attempts are recorded too, and the ordering must be tested, not assumed.

Use hash chaining with periodic batch anchoring (hourly/daily root hashes) to achieve tamper-evidence without per-event synchronous crypto overhead; sign root hashes with a key held outside the application.

Propagate correlation ids from the outermost entry point (API gateway) via headers (X-Request-ID, traceparent) through all synchronous and asynchronous processing, so distributed traces can be reconstructed from the audit log.
For high-throughput paths, use an async outbox or queue-based pipeline: write events to a local buffer first, then forward to the central sink; this decouples audit I/O from request latency.

Prune old events from hot storage to cold archival per retention schedules (SOX: ~7 years, HIPAA: ~6 years, GDPR: variable); ship to immutable object storage (S3 Object Lock, GCS Bucket Lock) for long-term tamper-evident retention.
Implement sequence numbering per service with gap detection in the sink to identify transmission losses or deliberate record deletion.

Use diff-based capture for entity updates (store only changed fields with old and new values) rather than full snapshots, to control storage volume and avoid logging sensitive fields that did not change.
Treat the interceptor binding configuration as a security-critical artifact: version-control it, require peer review to change it, and alert on unbindings or configuration drift.
sources: Steel, Nagappan & Lai, Core Security Patterns: Best Practices and Strategies for J2EE, Web Services, and Identity Management (2005) — Audit Interceptor documented in Chapter 10 (Securing the Business Tier) alongside Secure Logger; establishes the pattern's canonical intent, participants, and pairing with Secure Logger. http://coresecuritypatterns.websecuritypatterns.com/TOC-R1.htm

Heyman, Scandariato & Joosen (KU Leuven), "Reusable formal models for secure software architectures" (WICSA/ECSA 2012) — formal model of the Audit Interceptor's trust assumptions: correct and tamper-proof configuration, full mediation of sensitive invocations, intact logger binding, and correct read-back routing. https://lirias.kuleuven.be/retrieve/8cf1c168-d080-48e2-b87e-00628e87a49e

System Shardening, "Audit Logging Architecture: Designing Tamper-Resistant, Compliance-Ready Audit Trails" — correlation-first interceptor design, push-based ingestion via shippers, immutable object-store destinations, hash chaining with batched validation, sequence-number integrity, and multi-tier retention. https://www.systemshardening.com/articles/cross-cutting/audit-logging-architecture/

Nazar Boyko, "Audit Logging and Activity Trails Guide" — hash chaining for tamper-evidence, anchoring strategies (append-only store, third-party timestamping, Merkle trees), synchronous vs. async write tradeoffs, outbox pattern, and sequencing requirements for multi-worker environments. https://www.nazarboyko.com/articles/audit-logging-and-activity-trails

CodifySaaS, "SaaS Audit Log Implementation: 7 Proven Best Practices" — layered interceptor/subscriber architecture (request-context layer + entity-lifecycle layer), diff-based logging, AsyncLocalStorage for actor context propagation, EF Core and TypeORM subscriber patterns, and batching for high-throughput paths. https://codifysaas.com/blog/saas-architecture/saas-audit-log-implementation-enterprise/

APIScout, "API Compliance: GDPR, SOX & HIPAA Guide 2026" — per-call user attribution, tamper-evident log storage, unique identity enforcement, separation of duties in API design, and framework-specific retention and data-residency requirements. https://apiscout.dev/guides/api-compliance-gdpr-sox-hipaa-2026

JesseRules, MillWorks.AuditCore (.NET) — storage-layer audit interceptor using EF Core SaveChangesInterceptor with HMAC/hash-chain integrity, per-entity-type redaction (IAuditFieldRedactor), and configurable fail-closed behaviour for regulated entities (HIPAA, FERPA, PCI-DSS). https://github.com/jesseRules/MillWorks.AuditCore

Harshad Sonawane, "Audit Logging in Java Microservices: Techniques and Compliance Tips" — Spring AOP interceptor patterns, outbox pattern for async delivery, OpenTelemetry/Micrometer integration, and compliance mapping (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS, SOX, ISO 27001). https://harshad-sonawane.com/blog/audit-logging-in-java-microservices-techniques-and-compliance-tips/

Oracle / Java EE Documentation, "Intercepting Filter Pattern" — J2EE servlet filter chain as a canonical interceptor-chain implementation; declarative filter configuration via deployment descriptors and runtime ordering. https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/intercepting-filter.html

StackPractices, "Intercepting Filter Pattern" — filter chain vs. decorator vs. chain-of-responsibility comparison; stateless filter design, ordering documentation, and short-circuit-on-failure guidance. https://stackpractices.com/patterns/intercepting-filter-pattern/

Core Security Patterns catalog index — identifies Audit Interceptor in the Chapter 10 business-tier security patterns and pairs it with Secure Logger. http://coresecuritypatterns.websecuritypatterns.com/patterns.htm

Hibernate ORM documentation, "Envers" — @Audited entities receive _AUD history rows on transaction commit; custom revision entities/listeners can add actor metadata and audit strategies trade write cost for query speed. https://docs.hibernate.org/orm/5.1/userguide/html_single/chapters/envers/Envers.html

Django documentation, django.contrib.admin.models — LogEntry records action_time, user, object, addition/change/deletion flag and change_message for admin activity. https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.0/_modules/django/contrib/admin/models/

collectiveidea/audited, Audited README — Rails ActiveRecord extension that creates audit rows for model create/update/destroy operations, records changed attributes and can attribute the acting user. https://github.com/collectiveidea/audited

Jakarta EE Tutorial, Using Jakarta EE Interceptors — managed-class @AroundInvoke interceptors are explicitly used for auditing and call InvocationContext.proceed() around target execution. https://jakarta.ee/learn/jakartaee-tutorial/current/supporttechs/interceptors/interceptors.html

NIST SP 800-92, Guide to Computer Security Log Management — warns that logs may contain PII, requires protection and synchronized clocks, and treats generation, transmission, storage and retention as a design problem. https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-92.pdf

related_patterns_notes.interceptor: The Audit Interceptor is a concrete specialisation of the Interceptor pattern with a specific security-auditing purpose. The general Interceptor pattern provides the mechanics (intercept, optionally modify, delegate), while the Audit Interceptor adds the accountability semantics and structured event emission.
related_patterns_notes.intercepting-filter: Closely related; Intercepting Filter operates at the HTTP pipeline / request-response boundary and is a natural placement for audit interceptors at the API gateway layer. Both interpose on inbound requests, but Audit Interceptor focuses on structured security-event recording with a defined schema and correlation semantics, whereas Intercepting Filter is a general preprocessing/postprocessing chain (authentication, compression, validation). They compose: the audit interceptor can be a filter in the chain.
related_patterns_notes.secure-logger: The canonical pairing: Audit Interceptor emits events, Secure Logger receives and durably, tamper-evidently stores them. Audit Interceptor is the producer; Secure Logger is the sink with integrity guarantees. The pair is described together in Steel, Nagappan & Lai (Core Security Patterns, Chapter 10).
related_patterns_notes.decorator: The Audit Interceptor can be viewed as a specialised Decorator: it wraps the target with additional audit behaviour while preserving the original interface. Unlike a general Decorator, an Audit Interceptor is declarative (bound via annotation/pointcut), policy-driven (what to log, redaction rules), and typically does not modify the wrapped behaviour — it only observes and records.
related_patterns_notes.chain-of-responsibility: Interceptor chains (e.g., servlet filters, middleware pipelines, Jakarta EE interceptors) implement Chain of Responsibility. The Audit Interceptor is one link in that chain. Its ordering relative to other links matters: audit should wrap (not be wrapped by) authorization so denied attempts are recorded; authentication typically runs before audit so the actor identity is known.
related_patterns_notes.secure-base-action: Both are security-pattern participants: Secure Base Action encapsulates a set of security actions with their own security context, while Audit Interceptor observes those actions. In a layered security architecture, Secure Base Action performs the authorisation decision and Audit Interceptor records it.
related_patterns_notes.reference-monitor: Reference Monitor enforces access control decisions; Audit Interceptor records them. Together they provide defence-in-depth: Reference Monitor prevents unauthorized access, Audit Interceptor makes both authorised and denied attempts visible for accountability. The interceptor is a detective control; Reference Monitor is a preventive control.
related_patterns_notes.outbox-pattern: The Outbox Pattern is a complementary implementation technique for async audit pipelines: instead of writing directly to the sink (which couples the business transaction to sink availability), the interceptor writes to a local outbox table/queue, and a separate process forwards events to the central audit sink. This decouples audit I/O from request latency while guaranteeing at-least-once delivery.
related_patterns_notes.event-sourcing: Event Sourcing stores domain events as the system of record for state reconstruction; Audit Interceptor records security context around invocations. They can compose, but domain events alone do not guarantee actor attribution, denied-attempt coverage, redaction or tamper-evident retention.
